title: "Drafting the SPEC with an AI agent"

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

> tflplanner is experimental: the screens and functions may change. This
> article follows the screens of the development version (`next`).

> **What's new for 11/9**
>
> - The agent now builds and checks each report itself, and fixes what it
>   finds (see [Build and check](#build-check)).
> - Hints learned from your past TFLs, kept for every study (see
>   [Company hints](#company-hints)).
> - A short check to run on the company PC before the test (see
>   [Before 11/9](#before-1109)).

The **AI drafts** tab hands the study's materials (the TOC, the annotated
shells, the ADaM, the ADaM spec, the SAP) to an AI agent in your editor. The
agent writes a draft SPEC for each report and asks in its chat where the
materials do not settle a decision. tflplanner checks the drafts, copies the
ones you choose into the study, and makes the reports from them.

This article walks through the flow with the **AI sample**: a fictional study
(DMY-001, Example Pharma) with eight reports, made in one click. Everything in
it is fictional, and it holds no answers: the agent writes the SPEC.
The Japanese edition is [AI 連携の使い方](ja-ai-flow.html).

## What you need

- R 4.1 or later.
- An editor with an AI agent in **agent mode**, one of:
  - VS Code with GitHub Copilot (agent mode in its chat), or
  - Claude Code (the Claude desktop app's Code tab, or its VS Code extension).
- Opus or Fable: see [Recommended AI setup](#ai-setup) and [Which model](#models).
- The tflplanner home **inside a folder the editor can open**. The agent
  reads only the study's `ai/` folder, which the editor opens as a folder.

## 1. Install and set up (once)

```{r}
install.packages("remotes")
ref <- "ai-test-2026-11-09"  # the trial's tag; use the one you were given
remotes::install_github(paste0("ichirio/rtfreporter@", ref), upgrade = "never")
remotes::install_github(paste0("ichirio/tflspec@", ref), upgrade = "never")
remotes::install_github(paste0("ichirio/tflplanner@", ref), upgrade = "never")
# what the sample's reports use
install.packages(c("cards", "cardx", "haven", "broom", "broom.helpers", "parameters",
                   "dplyr", "tidyr", "readxl", "officer", "ggsurvfit", "patchwork"))

tflplanner::setup_tflplanner(home = "C:/work/tflplanner-home", language = "en")
tflplanner::add_shortcut()   # a desktop shortcut that starts the app
```

Use the tag you were given (or `next` for the development version). Start
the app with the shortcut or `tflplanner::run_app()`.

## Recommended AI setup {#ai-setup}

Read this before you start the agent in [step 2](#step-2).

| Level | Setup |
|---|---|
| **Verified** | The Claude desktop app's Code tab (Claude Code) with Opus or Fable. VS Code + GitHub Copilot (agent mode) with Fable, run on a company PC on 2026-11-02. |
| **Expected to work, not yet tested** | VS Code + Copilot with Opus (Opus was tested in Claude Code only). The Claude Code extension for VS Code (the same engine as the Code tab; not separately verified). Cursor and other agent tools that can read and write files in the study's `ai` folder and run `Rscript`: follow B. |
| **Not verified** | GPT models in Copilot: do not treat them as equivalent to Opus or Fable. |
| **Not recommended** | Sonnet and Haiku (see [Which model](#models)). |

Choose a plan where Opus or Fable can be selected.

Requirements:

1. The editor opens the study's `ai` folder as its workspace, so the agent
   works inside it alone ([step 2](#step-2)).
2. The agent can run `Rscript` in the terminal. If it cannot, set the review
   depth to **None** and run `run.R` yourself (see [Build and check](#build-check)).
3. VS Code + Copilot only. In Settings (Ctrl+, and search the name; see
   [VS Code AI settings](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/reference/ai-settings.md)):
   - `github.copilot.chat.summarizeAgentConversationHistory.enabled`: on (the default);
   - `chat.agent.maxRequests`: raise it from 25 to, for example, 1000;
   - `chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove`: add `"/^Rscript /": true`;
   - if your organization locks a setting, ask IT.
4. Check these on your PC before a real study (see [Before 11/9](#before-1109)).

**A. The Claude desktop app, Code tab**

1. Open the Code tab and, under the prompt box, choose the study's `ai` folder
   as the project folder.
2. In the model picker, choose Opus or Fable.
3. Paste the prompt as in [step 2](#step-2). Answer its questions in the chat;
   at each stop it shows a menu: reply `c` (the next request), a number such
   as `5` (the next 5 together) or `a` (all the rest together). Allow
   `Rscript` the first time it asks, so that it can build and check.

**B. VS Code, with GitHub Copilot (agent mode) or the Claude Code extension**

1. Open the `ai` folder as in [step 2](#step-2).
2. Open the chat. In Copilot, choose the agent mode and the model (Fable
   verified; Opus expected). In the Claude Code extension, click the model
   name under the prompt box.
3. Copilot only: set the three settings of requirement 3.
4. Then paste the prompt as in [step 2](#step-2), answer, and reply `c` / a
   number / `a` at each menu, as in A.

## 2. Make the study from the AI sample

1. On the **Studies** tab, press **New study...** (with no study yet, the
   start page has **The sample for the AI tab...**).
2. Under **Start from**, choose **The sample for the AI tab**.
3. Keep the study ID (`DMY-001`) or type your own, and press **Create**.

The study is made at once, in `studies/<ID>` under the home, and opened:

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| `docs/toc.xlsx` | The TOC (8 reports) |
| `docs/shells.xlsx` | The annotated shells (6 sheets, one shell a sheet) |
| `docs/adam_spec.xlsx` | The ADaM spec (Pinnacle 21 form) |
| `data/adam/` | 5 ADaM datasets (adsl, adae, adlb, advs, adtte) |
| `ai/docs/sap.docx` | The SAP, as a reference for the agent |

The materials leave some decisions open on purpose, to see whether the agent
asks instead of deciding silently.

## 3. Step 1: Write the prompt {#step-1}

The **AI drafts** tab opens on **1 Write the prompt**, with **The open study**
chosen and the fields filled: the TOC / SHELL workbook, the shell workbooks,
the ADaM folder (it says "5 files" under it), the ADaM spec, and `sap.docx`
under **Add a reference**. Each **Browse...** opens in the study's folder.

1. Press **Read and check**. The right side shows what was read: 8 TOC items,
   6 shells, the ADaM summary sent to the agent, and the workbook's sheets.
2. In **Sheets**, move `General conventions` (rules common to every report) to
   **Other sheets (not shells)** and press **Apply and read again**; then
   choose it in **Sheets for every request** on the left, so every request
   carries it.
3. Press **Write the requests**. The requests and the agent's prompt are
   written into the study's `ai/` folder.

> **Without the app.** Steps 2 and 3 can be run from R. This makes the same
> study and writes the same requests as the buttons above:
>
> ```{r}
> made <- tflplanner::create_ai_sample_study()   # New study > The sample for the AI tab
> kit <- made$kit
> p <- tflspec::tfl_ai_prepare(
>   dir = made$study$path, toc = kit$toc, adam = kit$adam,
>   shells = kit$shells, adam_spec = kit$adam_spec, docs = kit$docs,
>   sheet_roles = c("General conventions" = "other"),   # Sheets: move to Other
>   sheets = "General conventions",                     # Sheets for every request
>   dry_run = TRUE)                                      # Read and check
> # Write the requests: the same call with dry_run = FALSE
> ```
>
> - `kit$toc`, `kit$shells`, `kit$adam`, `kit$adam_spec` and `kit$docs` fill
>   the TOC / SHELL workbook, the shell workbooks, the ADaM folder, the ADaM
>   spec and **Add a reference**.
> - `dry_run = TRUE` is **Read and check** (nothing is written); with
>   `dry_run = FALSE` the call is **Write the requests**, and the drafts go to
>   `ai/spec/outputs/` (`area = TRUE`, the default).
> - `sheet_roles` is **Other sheets (not shells)** and **Apply and read
>   again**; `sheets` is **Sheets for every request**.
> - The app calls it with `quiet = TRUE`; leave that out to see the printout.

## 4. Step 2: The agent writes the SPEC {#step-2}

1. On **2 The agent writes the SPEC**, press **Copy the prompt**.
2. Open the study's **`ai` folder** in the editor (`studies/DMY-001/ai`; in VS
   Code, double-clicking `ai/DMY-001.code-workspace` does the same). Do not
   open the study folder or `studies/` above it.
3. Put the chat in agent mode, paste the prompt and send it.

The agent works request by request. It writes its drafts into
`ai/spec/outputs/`, and its decisions into `ai/decisions.md`. Where the
materials do not settle something, it writes to you, in one numbered message
for each request:

- **It decides** where the TOC, the shells, the SAP and the ADaM spec agree.
  It records the decision as an assumption on the draft.
- **It asks you to confirm a default** where the materials disagree, for
  example a TOC that names one analysis set and the SAP another. Each
  question gives the report, what each document says (sheet, section), the
  default it would take and why, and the other choices.
- **It asks** where nothing in the materials answers, still with a default.

Answer in the chat, briefly ("1: FAS, 2: the raw data's digits + 1"). After
each request the agent stops with a menu: reply `c` (the next request), a
number `N` (the next N together) or `a` (all the rest together, with all
its questions asked at the end of that batch). The select **How the agent
works through the requests** in [step 1](#step-1) sets this (**One request at
a time**, the default, or **Everything together**). If it stops for another
reason, send "continue". If it starts installing packages or searching folders,
send "Follow AGENTS.md: only write the drafts."

## 5. Step 3: Check the SPEC

On **3 Check the SPEC**, press **Check** (you can press it while the agent is
still working). Each draft gets:

- **ERROR**: the SPEC does not read; it cannot be copied.
- **WARNING**: it reads, but no program can be made from it yet.
- **OK**: a program can be made.

For an ERROR or a WARNING, copy the fix text on its row, paste it into the
same chat, and check again once the agent has fixed it.

## 6. Step 4: Copy into the study, and make the reports

1. On **4 Copy into the study**, tick the reports to take (at first, the
   drafts not adopted yet are ticked) and press **Adopt (copy) the reports
   ticked into the study**. They go onto the study's Report list.
2. Where the agent assumed something, its assumptions and the points **to
   confirm** are listed with each report. Mark each as right or wrong; what is
   wrong can be sent back to the chat as a correction request.
3. Make the reports (the **Runs** tab, **Run all**) and open the RTFs.

## Build and check {#build-check}

After the drafts of each request, the agent runs `Rscript run.R <request>`.
That makes the reports from the drafts. The agent then reads, against the
shell:

- `ai/status.md`,
- the program `<id>.R`,
- the facts text `<id>-facts.txt`,
- and, for a figure, the PNG.

It fixes at most twice. After that, a figure falls back to the agent's own
ggplot2 code, and a table is marked "to confirm".

How far this goes is set by the **Review depth** selects on the AI tab. They
are in step 1, under **Language**. The defaults are figures 3, tables 2,
listings 1.

| Level | The agent checks |
|---|---|
| 0 | Only that the report builds |
| 1 | + the program |
| 2 | + the facts |
| 3 | + the output (the PNG for a figure) |

**None** means the agent does not run anything: the person runs `run.R`. The
choice is saved in `study.yml` as `ai: review`.

Measured on the sample: about 110-120k tokens per 5 reports, at any level.

## Company hints, learned from past TFLs {#company-hints}

The agent can learn how your company's TFLs usually look.

1. Put the past TFLs (RTF) in `<home>/ai/past_tfl/`. `<home>` is the
   tflplanner home folder.
2. Run the learning step from the **Past reports' look** card on the AI tab,
   or in R:

```{r}
tflspec::tfl_ai_style_prompt(standard = company_standard)
```

3. Give the agent `AGENTS-learn.md`.

The agent writes `<home>/ai/company_hints.yml`. Anything that conflicts with
the company standard goes under `conflicts:`, never into the hints.

Every study prepared afterwards reads the hints. The order of authority:

1. the shell, the SAP and the company standard;
2. the hints;
3. usual practice;
4. then the agent asks.

Weak hints are marked "to confirm".

The card can also show what was learned against the company standard, line
by line. Tick the lines to adopt, then build a reference pack. This is
optional: a way to start a company standard.

## Before 11/9: a check on the company PC {#before-1109}

Do these on the company PC, in the editor you will use.

1. Ask the agent to run `Rscript --version` in its terminal. If it may not
   run commands, the person runs `run.R` (set the review depth to **None**).
2. Ask it to open a built PNG and describe it. If it can't open images, the
   facts text (`<id>-facts.txt`) covers the figure.
3. Check that tflspec is installed in the R that the terminal finds:

```
Rscript -e 'packageVersion("tflspec")'
```

## Which model {#models}

From a comparison on this sample (8 reports; the two hardest requests run
three times each; the same answers given in every run):

- **Use Opus or Fable.** Their results were equal within the noise of three
  runs: the same questions, defaults that agreed with the SAP and the define,
  no silent wrong decision, and the kit's rules kept. Choose between them by
  cost.
- **Sonnet and Haiku are not recommended** with the current kit. Sonnet chose
  a derivation wrongly in two runs of three (once silently, once as a wrong
  default), and rewrote requests whose drafts were already done. Haiku asked
  good questions, but repaired failed drafts by guessing, and its questions
  seldom said how the answer changes the numbers or why the default.
- **The editor made no difference** where it was tested: Fable gave the same
  result in VS Code with GitHub Copilot and in Claude Code (the same
  questions, all 8 reports made at the first try). Opus was tested in Claude
  Code only; the same is expected in Copilot, but it is not tested yet.

## What to expect of the drafts

- The drafts are **drafts**: a programmer reviews (QCs) every adopted report,
  as for one written by hand. The agent works from the materials it is given;
  where they are wrong or silent, so may the draft be.
- What the agent decided is never hidden: its assumptions and the points to
  confirm are on each report in step 4, and in `ai/decisions.md`. Read them
  first: they are where a draft is most likely to differ from what you meant.
- Some reports need a fix or two before they check OK; the shift tables were
  the hardest for every model.
